summary: This memo lists, as best known at the time, common Internet country domains and how they correspond to telex answerback codes, along with telex and international dialing codes where available. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Before the Internet was everywhere, many businesses used telex machines with short codes for each country. This paper is a lookup table matching those codes to Internet country endings.

questions: telex country codes and internet domains
telex answerback code to country domain
subtitle: A reference mapping of country telex codes to Internet domains

tldr.problem: In 1992, the Internet used country domain codes (like .uk, .de) while the global telex system used different telex answerback codes. Businesses and mail systems needed to map between them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC publishes a comprehensive table listing, for each country: the telephone country code, telex country code, telex answerback code, and Internet country domain. It also documents BITNET, UUCP, and other network addressing conventions.
tldr.outcome: It provided a practical reference at a moment when multiple communication systems coexisted. As email replaced telex and the Internet became dominant, the telex codes became archival, but the Internet domain mappings remain useful for understanding country-code domains.

today: RFC 1394 is primarily archival. Telex as a communication system became obsolete in the 1990s, making the telex codes historical. However, the Internet country domain mappings remain useful for understanding how the Domain Name System assigned country-level identifiers. Some entries (like .su for the former Soviet Union) document historical allocations no longer in use. The document is a snapshot of a moment when multiple international communication systems coexisted, before the Internet unified most of them.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 1394 is a reference document published in January 1993. It lists every known Internet country domain and maps it to international communication codes: telephone country codes, telex country codes, and telex answerback codes.

The document reflects a time when the Internet was not yet the dominant global communication system. Telex machines were still in use for official and business messages. Fax machines were increasingly common. Email was growing but not universal. The Internet had assigned two-letter country domain identifiers (like .uk for United Kingdom, .de for Germany), but these were new and not widely mapped to the older telex and phone systems that most organizations used.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a reference book. It shows how to write a country code in different ways depending on what system you are using—telephone, telex, or Internet.

sections.title: How to Use the Table
sections.content:
The main part of the RFC is a long alphabetical table organized by country or region. Each row lists: the name of the country, the telephone country code (for voice calls), the telex country code, the telex answerback code, and the Internet domain.

The RFC documents that some entries are incomplete or uncertain, marked with dashes when information is unknown or not applicable. An entry ending with a comma indicates that additional entries follow on the next line with the same prefix. The document's authors acknowledge that accuracy is not guaranteed and welcome corrections.

The table includes not just countries but also regions (like US states), special territories, ocean-based Inmarsat satellite systems, and online services (like America Online and Compuserve, which had their own email domain names at the time). It even lists major business telex networks like AT&T's ATTMAIL and MCI's MCIMAIL.
sections.plainLanguage: Find your country in the list, and you can see all the codes for it: phone, telex, and Internet. If you do not see your country, the next entries might be there under a different name.

sections.title: Codes and Addressing Systems
sections.content:
Telephone country codes (like 44 for the UK, 33 for France) are the prefixes you dial for international phone calls. Telex country codes are two- or three-digit routing codes used by the telex network to direct messages. Telex answerback codes identify the specific terminal or service within a country, typically two or three letters (like G for the UK, F for France).

Internet domain codes are the country-level top-level domains (like .uk, .de, .fr). These were assigned by IANA following ISO 3166 country codes, though some abbreviations predate the standard (like .su for the Soviet Union, later replaced).

The RFC also documents non-country domains for organizations: .edu for educational institutions, .com for commercial, .gov for government, .mil for military, .org for non-profit, .net for network providers, and .int for international organizations. It notes that users on BITNET, FIDONET, and UUCP networks often had to use special gateway addresses and percent-sign encoding to route mail between systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Each system has its own way of writing a country: phone uses numbers, telex uses codes, Internet uses letter pairs. This paper shows them all side by side.

sections.title: International Communication in 1993
sections.content:
The RFC reflects the state of global communication at a specific moment. Telex, though declining, was still important for official government and financial messages. International phone dialing was routine for businesses. The Internet was rapidly growing but had not yet become the default for personal communication.

The document notes important social and political facts: some countries could not reach others due to political restrictions (US to Cuba, Arab countries to Israel). It disclaims any standing on the validity or names of countries, acknowledging that information is solicited from users and corrections are welcome.

The table documents online services like CompuServe, AOL, and UUNet that provided proprietary email and network services. Many of these names and services have since vanished. The document is thus a snapshot of a transitional moment, showing the Internet still competing for dominance alongside established systems.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper shows how the world talked to itself in 1993. Some of the codes and services in it no longer exist, but they were real and important at the time.
